transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you start by telling me what brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because I keep blowing up at people over nothing. I yelled at one of my employees for putting stock on the wrong shelf, and afterward I was shaking because that’s not how I usually treat people.
Has this kind of irritability and quick temper been a new thing over the past few weeks or months, or is it something you've noticed throughout most of your life?

No, this is new for me. I don’t usually lose my temper like that. Lately I’ve been blowing up over little things, like when that employee put stock on the wrong shelf, and afterward I was shaking and felt awful about it.
How long has this irritability and quick temper been going on—days, weeks, or longer?
About two weeks now, ever since the kitchen fire during our first weekend working on the house.
Since the kitchen fire, have you had any unwanted memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about that event?

Yes. It just pops into my head without warning. I’ll be doing something ordinary, like picking up a pan or opening a spreadsheet, and suddenly I can smell the smoke again and see the kitchen filling up like I’m right back there.
Have you found yourself avoiding certain places, activities, or even thoughts that remind you of the kitchen fire?

Yes. I’ve been avoiding the house as much as I can, and I can’t even look at the mortgage folder. Even the herbs on my patio remind me of that day. My chest tightens up, and I just can’t make myself go near any of it.
Since the fire, have you noticed times when you feel detached from yourself or your surroundings, like things aren't quite real, or like you're in a daze?

Sometimes at the store, it feels like I’m watching myself from a few feet away. The aisles and customers are there, but they don’t feel quite real, and I’m just moving through everything on automatic.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient developed a cluster of stress-related symptoms—intrusive re-experiencing (unwanted memories/flashbacks of the fire), avoidance of trauma-related cues (the house, mortgage folder, herbs), dissociative depersonalization/derealization (watching herself from a distance, feeling unreal), and new-onset irritability/hyperarousal—beginning immediately after a clearly identifiable traumatic event (the kitchen fire) and persisting for only about two weeks. The short duration (<1 month) following an acute traumatic stressor, in a person with no prior history of such symptoms, is most consistent with Acute Stress Reaction (F43.0) rather than PTSD (which requires symptoms >1 month) or Adjustment Disorder (which typically lacks the intrusive/dissociative re-experiencing phenomena and follows a stressor of lesser severity).

New-onset irritability and low tolerance for minor frustrations
Angry outburst at employee followed by shaking/remorse
